enrichment.short_title: Careless driving appeal on heavy braking after unexplained HGV skid

statutes_considered.title: Road Traffic Act 1988
provisions: section 3 (driving without due care and attention)

key_facts: Gary Bingham was prosecuted for driving an HGV without due care on the A1034 after a fatal collision; the charge was careless driving, not causing death.

Magistrates found the rear of the lorry swung on a right-hand bend, that heavy braking probably locked the wheels immediately before impact, and that braking in those circumstances was not the conduct of a reasonable driver.

They did not expressly find that the initial loss of control was itself careless, though they made findings excluding mechanical defect, road contaminants, and an identified cause for the initial skid.
Expert tachograph evidence and the appellant's concession that braking would make matters worse supported the finding of heavy braking after the skid began.
enrichment.procedural_posture: Appeal by way of case stated from magistrates' conviction to the High Court (Administrative Division).
enrichment.outcome: Appeal dismissed; the magistrates were held correct in law to convict on the basis of careless heavy braking after the initial skid, and costs of £2,000 were ordered.
enrichment.ratio: Where magistrates lawfully find heavy braking after an initial skid, a prosecution may treat the whole incident as one episode of careless driving; the 'agony of the moment' principle does not assist a driver whose emergency reaction is not shown to have been to an emergency of his own innocent creation, and a finding of heavy braking supported by tachograph evidence and the driver's own concession was not perverse.
legal_issues: Whether magistrates were entitled to find heavy braking as a fact
Whether heavy braking after an initial unexplained skid proved careless driving beyond reasonable doubt
Whether the agony of the moment principle applied where the initial loss of control was not attributed to driver fault
Whether the case was a Wright v Wenlock inference case or a narrower braking-response case

enrichment.short_title: Domestic manslaughter sentence reduced after guilty-plea offer credit
key_facts: Mr Parnham killed his wife with an iron bar during a domestic argument on 5 March 2001 after she had struck him first; medical evidence indicated about 73 blows, 44 to the head.
He initially claimed intruders had attacked them, was tried for murder, and was convicted of involuntary manslaughter because the jury found he lacked intent for murder.
He was sentenced to six years' imprisonment at Lewes Crown Court on 11 January 2002.

He had offered to plead guilty to manslaughter before trial, but the judge gave no credit for that offer and the sentence was held manifestly excessive compared with comparable involuntary manslaughter cases.
enrichment.procedural_posture: Renewed application for leave to appeal against sentence, followed by full appeal to the Court of Appeal (Criminal Division).
enrichment.outcome: Appeal allowed; sentence reduced from six years to four years' imprisonment, with liberty to apply reserved.
enrichment.ratio: Some credit should be given for an offer to plead guilty to the offence ultimately convicted even where the prosecution rejected the offer and the trial proceeded on a fully contested basis; in domestic involuntary manslaughter cases lacking substantial mitigating features comparable to Higgins, a six-year sentence may be manifestly excessive where the offender did not intend death or really serious bodily harm.
legal_issues: Whether the judge erred in failing to give credit for an offer to plead guilty to manslaughter
Whether six years was manifestly excessive for involuntary manslaughter in a domestic context
How sentences for involuntary manslaughter compare with manslaughter by provocation

enrichment.short_title: Admissibility of complainant background evidence in indecent assault trial

statutes_considered.title: Youth Justice and Criminal Evidence Act 1999

key_facts: Steven Tobin was convicted at Chester Crown Court of two counts of indecent assault on a 16-year-old complainant in his car after she had been drinking in public houses.
The central issue was whether the complainant initiated oral sex while he drove, as he claimed, or whether he forced her, as she alleged.
The prosecution called limited evidence from the complainant's mother about the complainant's background, politeness, and distress after the incident.
The defence objected that this amounted to impermissible oath-helping, but the Court of Appeal held the trial was fair and the conviction safe.
enrichment.procedural_posture: Appeal against conviction with leave on one ground and renewed applications for leave on two further grounds.
enrichment.outcome: Appeal dismissed on the granted ground; leave refused on grounds 2 and 3.
enrichment.ratio: In sexual offence trials where credibility is decisive and the dispute goes directly to whether the complainant would have acted as alleged, limited prosecution evidence of a complainant's background and characteristics may be admissible even if it also bolsters credibility, provided it does not amount to general oath-helping that the witness is truthful; fairness may permit such evidence where the defendant's character has been fully explored.
legal_issues: Whether prosecution evidence of the complainant's good character and background was impermissible oath-helping
Whether the judge's summing-up invited the jury to treat the mother's evidence as proof of truthfulness
Whether the defence should have been granted an adjournment to investigate the complainant's character
Whether judicial questioning of the defendant improperly entered the arena

enrichment.short_title: Sea Empress whelk processor denied IOPC Fund pure economic loss claim

statutes_considered.title: Food Protection (Emergency Prohibitions)(Oil and Chemical Pollution of Fish and Plants) Order 1996 (SI 1996 No. 448)

key_facts: After the Sea Empress grounded at Milford Haven in February 1996, a fishing ban prevented Welsh whelk catches that supplied R J Tilbury & Sons' processing business in Devon.
The claimants sought recovery from the International Oil Pollution Compensation Fund 1971 for loss of gross profits of about £746,632 on a preliminary issue.
They had contracts with Welsh fishing vessels and Korean buyers for Welsh whelks that could not be replaced from other fisheries.
David Steel J held, and the Court of Appeal affirmed, that this was secondary or relational pure economic loss outside the statutory conception of damage caused by contamination.
enrichment.procedural_posture: Appeal with permission from a preliminary issue trial determining whether assumed loss of profits was recoverable damage under Schedule 4 to the Merchant Shipping Act 1995.
enrichment.outcome: Appeal dismissed; the whelk processor's economic loss was held not to be damage caused by contamination within section 153.
enrichment.ratio: Under the oil pollution compensation scheme, liability for damage caused by contamination is closely focused on physical contamination and its proximate consequences; a processor in Devon who lost profits because local fishermen could not supply whelks from contaminated waters suffered indirect relational economic loss comparable to Landcatch and outside the intended scope of the statute, even though existing supply contracts distinguished the facts superficially.
legal_issues: Whether loss of profits from inability to obtain Welsh whelks constitutes damage caused by contamination under section 153
How Landcatch Ltd v International Oil Pollution Compensation Fund applies to downstream processors
Whether common law rules on recovery of pure economic loss govern construction of the statutory scheme
Where to draw the line between recoverable fishermen's losses and non-recoverable relational losses

enrichment.short_title: Kosovo gay asylum claimant failed Article 3 and 8 removal challenge
key_facts: S, a Kosovo Albanian who arrived aged 17 in January 2000, raised a late claim of persecution on grounds of homosexuality during his asylum appeal and later pursued human rights claims.
The Special Adjudicator doubted he was homosexual but in judicial review the court proceeded on the assumption that he was.

Expert and background material indicated conservative social attitudes, possible discrimination, and legal uncertainty over homosexual conduct in Kosovo, but not a substantial risk of Article 3 ill-treatment.
Fresh evidence from Mr Standish at the hearing did not establish removal would breach Articles 3 or 8.
enrichment.procedural_posture: Claim for judicial review of an Immigration Appeal Tribunal decision refusing leave to appeal against a Special Adjudicator's dismissal of human rights claims.
enrichment.outcome: Claim for judicial review dismissed; removal held lawful and not in breach of Articles 3 or 8, and permission to appeal refused.
enrichment.ratio: Following Ullah and Z, Convention rights other than Article 3 generally do not prevent removal unless conduct in the destination state reaches the Article 3 threshold; social ostracism, verbal harassment, and conservative attitudes toward homosexuality in Kosovo, even on assumed homosexual orientation, did not establish a real risk of torture or inhuman or degrading treatment, and Article 8 did not require the United Kingdom to guarantee protection from non-flagrant social prejudice.
legal_issues: Whether removal of a gay Kosovo Albanian would breach Article 3
Whether Article 8 prevented removal where private life in the UK was engaged
Whether the Special Adjudicator adequately assessed objective country evidence
Whether Ullah and Z conflict on extraterritorial Article 8 protection
linked_authorities: SSHD v Z; M & A v SSHD

enrichment.short_title: Article 8 claim failed where spouse married during precarious immigration status
key_facts: Surinder Singh, an Indian asylum seeker whose claim failed, married a Malaysian national in April 2001 while his immigration status remained precarious.
His wife and three stepchildren, all long resident in the United Kingdom, faced hardship if required to follow him to India but faced no legal bar to doing so.
The Adjudicator and Immigration Appeal Tribunal held that interference with family life was proportionate for immigration control.
The couple had known each other about a year and the marriage had lasted about one year at the time of the decision.
enrichment.procedural_posture: Application for judicial review, brought with permission, of an Immigration Appeal Tribunal decision refusing leave to appeal against an Adjudicator's Article 8 decision.
enrichment.outcome: Application dismissed; removal held proportionate and not a breach of Article 8.
enrichment.ratio: Under Mahmood and Strasbourg jurisprudence, Article 8 does not impose a general obligation to respect a couple's choice of residence; where a spouse married knowing of the other's precarious immigration status, that knowledge militates against a finding that exclusion violates Article 8, and obstacles to the family following the removed spouse to India were not insurmountable merely because relocation would be extremely difficult in practice.
legal_issues: Whether obstacles to the family relocating to India were insurmountable
Whether the decision-maker placed undue weight on marriage during precarious status
Whether the Adjudicator had to consider prospects of future entry clearance from India
Application of Mahmood propositions to Article 8 proportionality
linked_authorities: R v Secretary of State for the Home Department ex parte Mahmood
Abdulaziz, Cabales and Balkandali v United Kingdom

enrichment.short_title: Equitable Life audit negligence strike-out on GAR provision and sale claims
key_facts: Equitable Life sued Ernst & Young for audit negligence relating to 1997-1999 audits and alleged failure to require adequate provisions for guaranteed annuity rate options and Hyman litigation disclosures.
Equitable claimed it would have sold the business earlier and/or declared lower bonuses if proper GAR provisions had appeared in the statutory accounts.
E&Y applied to strike out or obtain summary judgment on most claims, arguing the losses were outside an auditor's scope of duty and causation.
Langley J struck out the lost-sale and loss-of-chance claims but gave Equitable a limited opportunity to reformulate the bonus declaration claims.
enrichment.procedural_posture: Interlocutory application to strike out or for summary judgment on draft re-amended particulars in audit negligence proceedings.
enrichment.outcome: Lost-sale and loss-of-chance claims struck out; bonus declaration claims identified as seriously flawed but not finally struck out pending possible repleading within a defined timescale.
enrichment.ratio: An auditor's contractual duty to certify true and fair accounts does not extend to liability for a subsequent fall in business goodwill or failure to sell the company; under SAAMCO principles, negligent failure to require GAR provisions may arguably found claims for distributions such as bonuses paid in reliance on overstated surplus, but not for the wider economic losses Equitable claimed from missing hypothetical sales after the Hyman litigation.
legal_issues: Scope of an auditor's duty of care regarding GAR provisions and FFA
Whether lost-sale and goodwill erosion claims fall within SAAMCO
Causation and whether directors would have sold or cut bonuses if larger provisions had been insisted upon
Whether bonus overpayment claims are analogous to unlawful dividend recovery cases
Admissibility and measure of loss after the House of Lords decision in Hyman

enrichment.short_title: NASS could stop support paid in error to ineligible in-country asylum seeker
key_facts: Ms Manzana, a Congolese asylum seeker, applied for NASS support in July 2001 using a standard acknowledgment letter altered to show an earlier asylum application date.
NASS approved support in October 2001 but later discovered she was an in-country applicant excluded from section 95 support by the regulations.
The Chief Asylum Support Adjudicator allowed her appeal, holding that once support had been granted it could only be discontinued under regulation 20.
The Secretary of State brought judicial review, arguing a person never eligible for section 95 support was not entitled to continued payment after the error was discovered.
enrichment.procedural_posture: Judicial review of a Chief Asylum Support Adjudicator decision allowing an appeal against termination of asylum support.
enrichment.outcome: Judicial review granted; the adjudicator's decision quashed and the appeal directed to be dismissed.
enrichment.ratio: Regulation 20 provides exhaustive grounds for discontinuing support only for persons who meet the eligibility criteria of section 95; where a person was never eligible because she was an excluded in-country applicant, NASS was not obliged to continue support after discovering the error, and section 114 together with the statutory scheme assumes support ceases automatically when eligibility criteria are not fulfilled.
legal_issues: Whether regulation 20 is the only route to discontinue asylum support once granted
Whether a person never eligible under section 95 retains a right to support after mistaken approval
How section 114 recovery provisions interact with termination of ineligible support
Whether Rootkin v Kent County Council prevents rescission of support decisions
linked_authorities: R v Asylum Support Adjudicator ex parte Hussain

confidence.notes: Statutory scheme and central issue are clearly analysed. Toulson J delivered the judgment.

enrichment.short_title: Crown Court may consecutive summary sentence to either-way committal sentence
key_facts: McGuiness pleaded guilty in the magistrates' court to handling stolen goods, triable either way, and driving while disqualified, triable summarily.
He was committed for sentence to Reading Crown Court under sections 3 and 6 of the 2000 Act.
The Crown Court sentenced him to 15 months for handling and six months consecutive for disqualified driving, totalling 21 months.
It was argued that section 7(1) prevented consecutive summary sentences that together exceeded magistrates' aggregate limits under section 133.
enrichment.procedural_posture: Renewed application for leave to appeal against sentence in the Court of Appeal (Criminal Division).
enrichment.outcome: Renewed application dismissed; the consecutive sentences were held lawful.
enrichment.ratio: Section 7(1) of the Powers of Criminal Courts (Sentencing) Act 2000 limits the Crown Court when sentencing summary offences committed under section 6 to what magistrates could impose for those summary offences alone, but it does not restrict making a section 6 summary sentence consecutive to a section 3 either-way sentence even where the combined total exceeds section 133 magistrates' limits.
legal_issues: Whether the Crown Court could make a summary offence sentence consecutive to an either-way committal sentence
Whether section 7(1) incorporates section 133 aggregate limits across mixed committals
How sections 3, 6, and 7 interact on committal for sentence

confidence.notes: Short judgment on a discrete statutory construction point with clear outcome.

enrichment.short_title: Parenting order upheld in principle but quashed as irrational on facts

statutes_considered.title: Powers of the Criminal Courts (Sentencing) Act 2000

key_facts: M, aged 13, was convicted of wounding after a park attack linked to a long-running neighbour dispute; her mother AM was made subject to a 12-month parenting order and a £30 compensation order.
AM appealed unsuccessfully to the Inner London Crown Court and then sought judicial review, arguing parenting orders were incompatible with the Convention and irrational in her case.
The Secretary of State intervened; the court held parenting orders were compatible with Articles 6 and 8 as preventive measures addressing youth crime.
On the facts, the pre-sentence report opposed a parenting order and M was otherwise of exemplary character, so the parenting order was quashed as irrational though the compensation order stood.
enrichment.procedural_posture: Application for judicial review of an Inner London Crown Court decision dismissing appeal against a parenting order and section 137 compensation order.
enrichment.outcome: Parenting order quashed on irrationality grounds; section 137 compensation order upheld; sections 8-10 of the Crime and Disorder Act 1998 held compatible with the Convention.
enrichment.ratio: Parenting orders are preventive civil measures designed to reduce youth reoffending and are compatible with Articles 6 and 8 where the statutory conditions are met and the court evaluates desirability in the interests of preventing further offending; however, a parenting order may be quashed as perverse where the youth offending team considered the parent unsuitable, the offence arose from an isolated neighbour dispute, and the child was otherwise exemplary.
legal_issues: Whether parenting orders engage Article 6 and what standard of proof applies
Whether parenting orders are a necessary and proportionate interference with Article 8
Whether a parenting order was desirable in the interests of preventing further offending on these facts
Whether a section 137 compensation order was unreasonable where the parent was not at fault
